stories.title: Singapore’s Princeton Digital Group seeks US$1.2 bil loan for Malaysia data centre — Bloomberg
stories.summary: Asian data centre operator Princeton Digital Group Ltd is seeking a syndicated loan of up to US$1.2 billion (RM4.9 billion) to fund its Malaysia buildout, according to a person familiar with the matter, as the debt binge to finance artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure continues.
stories.why_it_matters: PDG's borrowing push shows the Malaysia land grab is shifting from equity-funded announcements to leveraged execution, raising the stakes on project delivery timelines. Bankers and rival operators should read this as evidence that syndicated debt markets — not just private capital — are becoming the primary funding channel for the region's AI capacity race.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
(Oct 14): Asian data centre operator Princeton Digital Group Ltd is seeking a syndicated loan of up to US$1.2 billion (RM4.9 billion) to fund its Malaysia buildout, according to a person familiar with the matter, as the debt binge to finance artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure continues.

HSBC Holdings plc Singapore branch, Maybank Investment Bank Bhd, OCBC Bank (Malaysia) Bhd, Standard Chartered Bank (Singapore) Ltd, and United Overseas Bank Ltd are the mandated lead arrangers and bookrunners for the three-year loan deal, said the person, asking not to be identified discussing private information.

Proceeds from the loan to be taken by the company’s subsidiary, Princeton Digital Group Labuan Alpha Ltd, will be used to fund a 198.8-megawatt data centre campus project in Johor, Malaysia, and to refinance existing debt, the person said.

Standard Chartered declined to comment. Representatives for Princeton Digital Group, HSBC, Maybank, OCBC Malaysia and UOB didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Data centre companies across the world have been taking on debt as they seek to raise capital to meet growing AI demand. Moody’s Ratings expects at least US$3 trillion to flow into data centre-related investments over the next five years, with much of the spending financed through debt.

But there are signs global investors are starting to push back against what they see are frothy AI valuations as evidenced by the collapse of Nvidia Corp-backed data centre operator Firmus Grid Ltd’s initial public offering last week.

Data centre firm AirTrunk, which counts Blackstone Inc as a key investor, was reported to delay its planned IPO of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until next year as higher interest rates and market volatility temper investor demand.

Headquartered in Singapore, Princeton Digital’s top shareholder is Warburg Pincus and other investors include Stonepeak Partners, Abu Dhabi sovereign fund Mubadala Investment Co and Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan Board.

The firm, founded in 2018, operates more than 1.8 gigawatts of data centre capacity across Asia including China, Japan, South Korea, India, Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia, according to its website.

PDG has been on a borrowing spree as it seeks to expand across Asia. In May, the firm said it raised around US$856 million for its data centre buildout in Indonesia. Earlier in the year, the company said it was targeting to raise US$5 billion in debt to support regional expansion plans.

stories.summary: CMC, the second-largest technology corporation in Vietnam, has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Lotte Innovate, a South Korean ICT and digital transformation service provider, to develop a variety of digital infrastructure including cloud and data center projects. In a press release, CMC revealed that the agreement identifies five priority areas of cooperation: […]
stories.why_it_matters: The pairing of a domestic champion with a Korean conglomerate's ICT arm fits Vietnam's pattern of using foreign partnerships to accelerate its data center buildout while keeping local ownership central. It adds to signs that Vietnam is positioning itself as the next regulated-market growth story in Southeast Asia after Malaysia and Indonesia, though MoUs of this kind frequently stall before reaching construction.
stories.content:
CMC, the second-largest technology corporation in Vietnam, has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Lotte Innovate, a South Korean ICT and digital transformation service provider, to develop a variety of digital infrastructure including cloud and data center projects.

In a press release, CMC revealed that the agreement identifies five priority areas of cooperation: Data Center, EV Charging, Security, Offshoring, and Cloud. It said that the two sides aim to develop data center projects, and when it comes to Cloud cooperation, it “is geared toward developing Vietnam’s cloud computing market, helping enterprises modernize their infrastructure and accelerate digital transformation.”

Minh Tran Van, CEO of CMC Korea, said, “Our partnership with Lotte Innovate goes beyond a step in CMC’s global expansion strategy. It reflects the growing role of CMC Korea in connecting Vietnam’s technology capabilities with Korea’s leading corporations. We expect the two sides to not only deliver high-quality software development services together, but also co-create scalable digital solutions across Vietnam, Korea, and regional markets, as demand for digital transformation and AI adoption continues to accelerate across the region.”

Choi Jong Pil, General Director of Lotte Innovate Vietnam, said, “Vietnam is a key market in Lotte Innovate’s global strategy. Through this partnership agreement with CMC Corporation, we aim to combine the strengths of both sides and explore new opportunities in advanced technology areas, contributing to digital transformation and AI adoption for businesses in Vietnam and the region.”

As per research by Arizton Advisory & Intelligence, the Vietnam data center market size was valued at US$ 1.04 billion in 2025, and is expected to reach US$ 3.19 billion by 2031, growing at a CAGR of 20.47 percent during the forecast period. It says that the market is driven by the growing adoption of digital platforms, advancements in technologies such as AI, expansion of the digital economy, rising internet usage and data traffic, government initiatives, and the increasing number of mobile and social media users.

stories.title: Bitdeer adds 127MW in Malaysia as AI cloud expansion gathers pace
stories.summary: Singapore-headquartered AI neocloud service provider Bitdeer AI has recently secured a combined 127MW of data center capacity in Malaysia, as it approaches 95 per cent of its target of up to 350MW by early 2028 across its global footprint. Its total combined capacity has now reached about 333.5MW across Malaysia, Norway and the United States, […]
stories.why_it_matters: Bitdeer's pace illustrates how neocloud providers spun out of the crypto-mining world are repurposing their power-procurement skills into AI capacity faster than many purpose-built rivals. Malaysia's emergence as the anchor of that growth intensifies competition for power and sites with hyperscale developers already flooding Johor.
stories.content:
Singapore-headquartered AI neocloud service provider Bitdeer AI has recently secured a combined 127MW of data center capacity in Malaysia, as it approaches 95 per cent of its target of up to 350MW by early 2028 across its global footprint. Its total combined capacity has now reached about 333.5MW across Malaysia, Norway and the United States, the firm said in two separate press releases.

So far this month, it has signed two AI cloud capacity agreements for its data centers in Malaysia. The secured headline capacity includes facilities owned or covered by its signed data center services agreements, and does not mean all that capacity is operating.

This follows Bitdeer’s announcement in September that it had obtained customer commitments for more than 70 per cent of its 21.7MW A201 facility in Johor, Malaysia, ahead of expected energisation in 1Q 2027. The firm added it had procured more than 100 racks of Nvidia GB300 NVL72 systems for deployment after energisation. Part of its A201’s rack space is designed to accommodate Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin platform.

Bitdeer estimates that revenue from the contracts might exceed US$1.7 billion over five years, lifting the company’s total expected revenue backlog to about US$2.9 billion. The firm expects to finance the development through customer prepayments, operating cash flow and borrowing secured against contracted cash flows.

The larger of the two October additions, A901, is a 67MW campus in an unspecified location in Malaysia, secured under a 10-year services agreement. It’s the firm’s third Malaysian hub alongside Cyberjaya and Johor. Delivery is expected in 1Q 2027 with full 67MW targeted for 2Q 2027.

The other October agreement is an eight-year services agreement for the 60MW A103 facility in Cyberjaya. Energisation is expected in 1Q 2028 for the facilty which is designed for liquid-cooled Nvidia systems, including Vera Rubin. Together with the A101 and A102 facilities, the Cyberjaya campus will represent about 71.5MW of AI Cloud data center capacity.

“We have secured approximately 95% of our up-to-350MW target with the addition of the A103 facility. Adding 60MW alongside the A101 and A102 facilities means we benefit from the power, the cooling and the network infrastructure already in place, improving our time-to-market. A103 is also built for the Vera Rubin generation, which is the capacity customers are asking us about for 2028,” said Michael G. Potter, Chief Financial Officer of Bitdeer Technologies Group.

“Demand for liquid-cooled, rack-scale AI capacity in Southeast Asia is running ahead of what the market can deliver, and customers are asking for it earlier and in larger blocks,” Potter added.

Bitdeer estimates its active AI cloud sales pipeline exceeds US$10 billion. Bitdeer is the AI cloud arm of Nasdaq-listed Bitdeer Technologies Group and is a preferred NVIDIA Cloud Partner.

stories.title: Foresight targets 270 MW Polish data center projects in proposed acquisition
stories.summary: Foresight Autonomous Holdings (Foresight), a technology company developing advanced 3D perception systems and cellular-based applications, has signed a non-binding term sheet to acquire a 50.01 percent controlling stake in a company developing two data center projects in Poland, with a combined planned power capacity of 270 MW. The press release did not identify by name […]
stories.content:
Foresight Autonomous Holdings (Foresight), a technology company developing advanced 3D perception systems and cellular-based applications, has signed a non-binding term sheet to acquire a 50.01 percent controlling stake in a company developing two data center projects in Poland, with a combined planned power capacity of 270 MW.

The press release did not identify by name the company that is targeted for acquisition, and referred to only as “The Data Centers Company”. This company is expected to hold a 66.67 percent interest in each project, located in Warsaw and Wroclaw. The remaining stakes will be held by Polish development partners.

The Warsaw project, located in Ożarów, comprises approximately 3.2 hectares of secured land, with a further 2.2 hectares available under an option, and is planned to have a total capacity of 130 MW. An application for grid connection has been submitted, with final approval currently expected by the end of 2027. The Wrocław project covers approximately 10 hectares and is planned to deliver a capacity of 140 MW, with the feasibility study already completed and land negotiations currently ongoing.

“As we previously announced, Foresight has been evaluating opportunities to expand into new technology markets and identify additional areas for growth beyond our existing activities, including data centers,” said, Haim Siboni, CEO, Foresight. “The proposed transaction is a natural extension of this strategy, providing Foresight with an opportunity to establish a controlling interest in a platform advancing two data center projects in Poland. At the same time, we continue to advance our proprietary technologies and expand their applications, including our recently announced development of full autonomous driving solutions for Unmanned Ground and Aerial Vehicles.”

The acquisition price will be based on an independent valuation by a mutually agreed firm. The purchase consideration will be financed entirely through a seller loan. Foresight also expects to contribute approximately US$ 1 million at closing toward its share of the target company’s outstanding shareholder loans. It has also committed to providing US$ 2.5 million in additional shareholder loans to support the projects.

To finance these commitments, the target company’s existing shareholders, or parties acting on their behalf, would provide Foresight with a convertible loan facility of up to US$ 3.5 million. The facility would be subject to an agreed budget, business plan and project milestones, with detailed terms to be set out in a separate agreement.

The proposed acquisition remains subject to due diligence, an independent valuation, definitive agreements and the necessary corporate, regulatory, stock exchange, governmental, financing and third-party approvals.

According to research by Mordor Intelligence, the Poland data center market size is expected to increase from 660 MW in 2025, to 702.52 MW in 2026, and eventually reach 998.34 MW by 2031, growing at a 7.28 percent compound annual growth rate (CAGR) between 2026 and 2031.

stories.title: AI demand drives modular data center prefabrication necessity
stories.summary: Accelerated compute for artificial intelligence (AI) clusters is changing data center design and deployment. Prefabrication has become essential due to challenging densities and a shortage of skilled tradespeople.
stories.content:
The demand for prefabricated data centers is accelerating significantly, driven by the race to build AI factory data centers. While modular data centers have existed for over 30 years, the current scale of deployment makes prefabrication a necessity.AI factory campuses can reach up to 10 gigawatts, requiring new planning and commissioning processes. Power densities for AI racks are close to 250 kilowatts, compared to 10-20 kilowatts for cloud data centers.Cooling for AI data centers is primarily liquid-based, a significant shift from traditional cloud data centers that typically lacked liquid cooling. These high power capacity, scale, and density requirements pose considerable planning and construction challenges for data center operators.
### Prefabrication advantages

Prefabrication significantly improves the probability of deploying AI factory data centers on schedule and achieving desired performance. Prefabricating uninterruptible power supply (UPS) and switchgear systems onto skids or enclosures offers faster delivery, factory-tested quality, and lower labour costs.Building these power units off-site reduces on-site labour needs and mitigates weather delays. The shortage of skilled electricians on-site is a growing concern for deploying these power systems.
### High-density liquid cooling

New racks, such as the AMD Helios 445 at 246 kilowatts per rack and the NVIDIA Vera Rubin at 227 kilowatts per rack, necessitate liquid cooling at scale. Liquid cooling began three years ago at around 70 kilowatts per rack and is rapidly expanding.The AI factory modular IT Pod is an innovation designed for high-density AI clusters. It integrates power and cooling components, including busway, power distribution, main piping, and piping to servers, above the AI racks in an overhead metal superstructure.Major components are factory-assembled, packed flat, and then assembled in the IT room. This approach differs from traditional skids or enclosures, reducing design and deployment time by bringing prebuilt modules directly into the AI factory IT room. Site preparation can occur in parallel with power module and IT Pod production, speeding up overall deployment.

stories.title: Ireland's Supreme Court clears €1.6bn Ennis data centre
stories.summary: Ireland's Supreme Court has rejected an appeal against the planning approval for Art Data Centres' proposed €1.6 billion campus outside Ennis, County Clare. This decision removes the final legal hurdle, allowing the 200MW data centre project to proceed after a lengthy challenge.
stories.content:
Ireland's Supreme Court has rejected a request to appeal the planning approval for Art Data Centres' proposed €1.6 billion campus near Ennis, County Clare. This decision brings an end to a prolonged legal challenge that sought to block the 200MW data centre development on environmental grounds.The court noted that the appeal application did not meet the constitutional threshold for further review. This follows the High Court's dismissal of a judicial review in March 2026 and its refusal of permission to appeal in May of the same year.The approved scheme includes six data centre buildings on a 145-acre site, an electricity substation, an energy centre, and facilities for vertical farming and heat reuse. Art Data Centres anticipates the project will support up to 1,200 construction jobs and 1,000 permanent jobs upon completion.
### Electricity Connection Challenges Remain

The project still requires a secured electricity connection to power the data centres, with construction expected to commence in 2027 once these arrangements are finalised. The approved plans incorporate a 110kV substation, a 120MW gas-fired generation facility, and 66 emergency diesel generators.New regulations from Ireland's energy regulator could affect the gas-fired generator, potentially making new gas connections for large industrial users interruptible during network pressure. The Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) also introduced new electricity connection requirements in December 2025.These new CRU rules mandate that applicants provide generation or storage capacity matching their maximum electricity import capacity, alongside renewable electricity covering at least 80 per cent of annual demand. However, the CRU's decision allows qualifying applications already in process to proceed under Ireland's earlier connection framework, which may benefit Art Data Centres due to its legal delays. The initial target for the first phase, including a substation and two data halls, was the end of 2028.

stories.summary: CtrlS Datacenters Ltd., a key player in South Asia’s data center landscape, has unveiled plans to invest Rs 10,000 crore (~US$ 1 billion) to set up a 150 MW hyperscale AI factory in Bodh Gaya, in the northern Indian state of Bihar. The company has signed a Letter of Intent (LOI) with the Government of […]
stories.content:
CtrlS Datacenters Ltd., a key player in South Asia’s data center landscape, has unveiled plans to invest Rs 10,000 crore (\~US$ 1 billion) to set up a 150 MW hyperscale AI factory in Bodh Gaya, in the northern Indian state of Bihar. The company has signed a Letter of Intent (LOI) with the Government of Bihar for this project.

The announcement was made on the sidelines of the inauguration of its new Rs 400-crore AI and cloud-ready data center in Patna, the capital city of Bihar. The inauguration took place in the presence of Bihar’s Chief Minister Shri Samrat Choudhary.

The greenfield facility currently offers an IT load of 12 MW with the potential to expand as per future demand. Located in the Patliputra Industrial Area, Patna, the company’s data center facility will support the growing digital infrastructure needs of enterprises, government institutions, hyperscalers and technology businesses in Bihar and Eastern India.

Sridhar Pinnapureddy, Founder & CEO, CtrlS Datacenters, said, “We are committed to strengthening Bihar’s digital infrastructure and building a robust IT ecosystem through our future-ready datacenters, designed to serve the evolving needs of hyperscalers, enterprises, and startups. We sincerely appreciate the Government of Bihar for creating a conducive policy environment, fostering an industry-friendly business climate, and providing attractive incentives that have supported our investment in the State.”

The company says that it is focused on building a hyper-connected network of data centers across India and beyond, extending reliable digital infrastructure closer to emerging demand hubs. As part of this strategy, the company plans to establish over 20 Edge datacenters across Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities in India over the coming years.

At present, CtrlS Datacenters Ltd, which began its operations in 2007, operates 19 data centers across nine key markets of India and is set to build over 4.4 GW of data center capacity by 2030. CtrlS Datacenters has announced its plans to explore new overseas markets in Southeast Asia and Middle East, with Thailand being the first international market foray.

stories.title: AI drives internet traffic shift, boosts data center demand
stories.summary: The surge in artificial intelligence has led to a notable shift in internet traffic patterns, with machine-generated requests exceeding human ones for the first time in June. This trend is increasing demand for data center capacity and infrastructure.
stories.content:
The current artificial intelligence (AI) climate has highlighted a significant industry shift, moving telecommunications from a siloed focus to an integral part of the digital ecosystem. The AI race has intensified the demand for power, data center capacity, and infrastructure, according to Avijit Singh of COLT at Capacity Europe.Cloudflare data from June revealed that machine-generated web page requests surpassed human requests, accounting for 57.4 per cent against 42.6 per cent. This milestone indicates a pivotal change in internet usage, moving from a design primarily for human consumption to one that must cater to agents.Singh projected that within five years, machine traffic could exceed human traffic by a factor of 100. This shift will alter traffic patterns, moving from north-south (cloud to user) to east-west (agent to agent, data center to data center).Network requirements will evolve, necessitating greater resilience, low latency, automation, observability, and fibre to prevent AI outages. Security checks will also shift emphasis from user verification to machine identity and authentication. Singh stressed that the value of networks will increasingly be measured by their relevance to intelligence rather than routing kilometres, advocating for innovation over mere transformation.Success in this evolving landscape will depend on effectively connecting compute, cloud regions, and power sources. This approach requires building ecosystems rather than maintaining silos, ensuring the industry connects intelligence, not just people.

stories.title: CDC offers AU$225 million community benefits for Wagga Wagga data centre
stories.summary: CDC Data Centres has proposed a community-benefits package worth up to AU$225 million for its planned 1.4GW data centre campus near Wagga Wagga, New South Wales. The package is conditional on the project being approved and proceeding as planned. This initiative aims to secure local support for the estimated AU$15 billion development.
stories.why_it_matters: Attaching a nine-figure benefits package to a planning application shows community opposition has become a material development risk for gigawatt-scale campuses in regional Australia, not just a PR issue. If the model works, expect rival developers to face pressure to match it, effectively adding a new line item to the cost of securing approvals for large regional sites.
stories.content:
CDC Data Centres has proposed a community-benefits package valued at up to AU$225 million for its planned 1.4GW data centre campus near Wagga Wagga, New South Wales (NSW). The Wagga Wagga City Council stated that any land sale would require a binding agreement of at least AU$150 million. This amount is equivalent to one per cent of the estimated AU$15 billion development cost.An additional AU$75 million has been proposed by CDC for community initiatives. These combined commitments could exceed AU$225 million. The entire package is conditional on the project receiving approval and proceeding as planned.CDC described the agreement as a proposed Voluntary Planning Agreement (VPA). Its final terms have not been published. The company indicated the funds could support housing, sport, recreation, arts, culture, education, skills, workforce development, environmental improvements, and community infrastructure. CDC also noted that local people would help identify priorities.
### Project scope and approvals

The proposed campus would include four data centre buildings at 216 Ashfords Road, Gregadoo, according to the scoping report. The council's land-sale resolution referred to 232 Ashfords Road. CDC estimates the development will cost approximately AU$15 billion and have a total power demand of up to 1.4GW. The project is intended to be built in stages with associated electrical and other infrastructure.CDC identified the area's proximity to existing transmission infrastructure as a factor in its site selection. The connection process has commenced with Transgrid through Lumea. CDC stated it would pay for its own electricity infrastructure, including any grid upgrades. However, the headline capacity remains a proposal, and CDC has not announced a final connection agreement for the proposed 1.4GW campus. The NSW Government will assess the development under its State Significant Development process. The council's authorisation of the land sale is separate from development consent.Community concerns have been raised regarding the project. CDC founder and CEO Greg Boorer emphasised the need for data centre developers to address community concerns as project scales grow. He stated that CDC data centres do not consume water for primary cooling and will not draw on local Riverina water supplies.

stories.title: LiNova CEO: UPS battery safety vital for data centers
stories.summary: Michael Nagus, CEO of LiNova, stated that data center operators must prioritize battery safety alongside capacity and cost during UPS upgrades. This focus is critical to prevent thermal runaway risks that can cause facility-wide crises.
stories.content:
Michael Nagus, CEO of LiNova, highlighted that data center operators must consider battery safety as a primary factor when upgrading uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems.He noted that while cyberattacks gain headlines, power failure remains the leading cause of data center outages. These failures often originate in backup systems designed to prevent them.Data centers underpin critical services like artificial intelligence (AI) and cloud platforms, where downtime costs can exceed $1 million per hour. Uptime expectations demand five-nines availability.
### Thermal Runaway Risks

The risk of thermal runaway in UPS batteries is no longer theoretical, with high-profile battery fires demonstrating rapid escalation into facility-wide crises. Nagus cited a 2025 data center fire in South Korea, triggered by a UPS system, which disabled government systems for 22 hours.Such incidents are prompting operators to re-evaluate battery safety across the entire lifecycle of backup power systems. This reassessment is crucial during UPS refresh cycles.Operators often focus on runtime, footprint, and energy efficiency during these cycles. However, refresh cycles also offer an opportunity to evaluate battery behavior under abuse scenarios, failure isolation, and early detection.Battery monitoring and maintenance are central to these discussions. Teams should assess whether monitoring systems provide real-time visibility into temperature, voltage, impedance, and cell-level anomalies.Maintenance strategies should include clear protocols for testing, replacement, and end-of-life management beyond scheduled inspections. Fire suppression and room design are also under greater scrutiny as energy storage deployments scale.Some facilities are incorporating additional compartmentalisation to prevent cascading failures. Others are redesigning battery rooms to align with evolving fire codes and insurance requirements.Alternative battery chemistries, such as lithium titanate oxide, nickel-zinc, and designs with non-metal or organic cathodes, are being explored to mitigate thermal runaway risks. Avoiding catastrophic failure is becoming a priority on par with performance and price.
### Business Implications

Choosing batteries with a lower risk of thermal runaway is an operational decision with business implications. Depending on the system and local requirements, such batteries may simplify permitting and inspections.They can also reduce insurance exposure and limit floor space dedicated to fire suppression and containment. This reclaimed space can then support revenue-generating infrastructure.Insurance providers are paying closer attention, evaluating how facilities assess and mitigate thermal risk. Operators may face higher premiums or additional compliance obligations if battery safety strategies are not clearly defined.Nagus emphasised that safety must be a top-tier decision factor, alongside cost per kWh and power density. Advances in battery materials and design suggest safety does not always compromise performance or affordability.

stories.title: Chiplets reshape server design, impacting data center efficiency
stories.summary: Chiplets, small modular dies, are changing how CPUs are built, improving manufacturing flexibility and enabling specialized processor designs. This shift could reshape data center approaches to compute density, power efficiency, and infrastructure planning.
stories.content:
Chiplets are beginning to reshape server design, moving away from traditional single-piece silicon microprocessors. These small modular dies can be combined in a single processor package, offering chipmakers a new way to build central processing units (CPUs). This approach enhances manufacturing flexibility and supports more specialized processor designs.The adoption of chiplets could influence how data centers manage compute density, power efficiency, and infrastructure planning. Chiplets are small integrated circuits designed for specific functions within a larger processing package. They can handle compute, input/output (I/O), cache, memory connectivity, or workload-specific acceleration, such as for artificial intelligence (AI).
### Impact on Data Center Operations

When combined, chiplets provide the same capabilities as a traditional CPU. However, they allow chipmakers to build processors from multiple smaller dies rather than one large monolithic die. This method can reduce manufacturing costs, as smaller dies are often easier to produce with higher yields. It also offers greater design freedom, enabling tailoring for different workloads and product segments.Chiplets may lead to higher compute density within data centers. If server vendors can deliver more processing power in a single server platform, operators might support heavier workloads without a proportional increase in physical footprint. While higher density typically means increased power draw and cooling, more efficient processor designs or better performance per watt from chiplets could offset some infrastructure strain.This approach could also enhance supply chain flexibility, potentially reducing server procurement delays. Smaller dies are often easier and faster to manufacture than large monolithic chips. In the longer term, chiplets could promote more specialized server designs, specifically tailored for workloads like AI, analytics, storage, or high-performance computing (HPC). This would offer data center operators more options but also require more workload-specific infrastructure planning.

stories.title: CDC offers Australian community AU$ 225m in proposed data centre benefits
stories.summary: CDC Data Centres has proposed a community-benefits package worth up to AU$ 225 million for its planned 1.4GW data centre campus near Wagga Wagga, NSW. Wagga Wagga City Council says any land sale would require a binding agreement worth at least AU$ 150 million, equivalent to at least one percent of the estimated AU$ 15 […]
stories.why_it_matters: The council's explicit one-percent floor turns community benefits from a voluntary goodwill gesture into a negotiated cost of land access, giving local governments across Australia a template to quantify their asks. Developers eyeing regional sites should now assume host communities will anchor negotiations to headline project values.
stories.content:
CDC Data Centres has proposed a community-benefits package worth up to AU$ 225 million for its planned 1.4GW data centre campus near Wagga Wagga, NSW. Wagga Wagga City Council says any land sale would require a binding agreement worth at least AU$ 150 million, equivalent to at least one percent of the estimated AU$ 15 billion development cost. Combined with a separate AU$ 75 million proposed by CDC for community initiatives, the commitments could exceed AU$ 225 million.

The package is conditional on the project being approved and proceeding as planned. CDC describes the agreement as a proposed Voluntary Planning Agreement (VPA), although its final terms have not been published.

CDC said the money could support housing, sport and recreation, arts and culture, education and skills, workforce development, environmental improvements and community infrastructure. The company said local people would have an opportunity to help identify priorities.

“This is not about building a data centre and walking away. We want to be part of Wagga Wagga’s future,” CDC founder and CEO Greg Boorer said in the announcement. “If this project proceeds, the community should see real, visible and lasting benefits from the investment.”

On 12 October, Wagga Wagga City Council authorised its general manager to enter into a contract to sell the land to CDC. The decision was made in a closed session. The proposed development remains subject to assessment by the NSW Government under its State Significant Development process.

### A major regional proposal

The proposed campus would comprise four data centre buildings at 216 Ashfords Road, Gregadoo, according to the scoping report. The council’s land-sale resolution refers to 232 Ashfords Road. CDC estimates the development would cost approximately AU$ 15 billion and have total power demand of up to 1.4GW.

The project is intended to be built in stages, with associated electrical and other infrastructure. CDC has identified the area’s proximity to existing transmission infrastructure as a factor in its site selection.

The scoping report says the connection process has commenced with Transgrid through Lumea. CDC says it would pay for its own electricity infrastructure, including any upgrades needed to connect to the grid.

However, the headline capacity remains a proposal rather than secured demand. CDC has not announced a final connection agreement for the proposed 1.4GW campus. The detailed infrastructure requirements are expected to be examined through the environmental assessment.

The community package follows residents seeking more information about the project. About Regional reported on 2 October that two petitions opposing the proposal had been launched within 24 hours of it becoming public. ABC News reported on 8 October on a mixed local response, including cautious support from advocacy group Committee 4 Wagga.

CDC says its data centres do not consume water for primary cooling purposes and will not draw on local Riverina water supplies. The detailed water-management plan is expected to form part of the environmental assessment.

### Boorer emphasises engagement

Boorer has recently spoken about the need for data centre developers to address community concerns as the scale of proposed projects grows. In an interview with ABC News published on 30 September, Boorer said CDC would hold community engagement and education sessions. He also expressed confidence that sourcing finance for the Gregadoo project would not be an issue, although no financial close or fully committed funding package for the development has been announced.

In an interview with About Regional published in October, Boorer described the proposal as a “once-in-a-generation opportunity” for Wagga Wagga and the wider Riverina. The outlet reported that local residents had raised concerns about the project’s potential impacts.

The benefits package is a more tangible proposal than general statements about potential economic impact, but its value to the region will depend on its final terms, the timing of contributions and whether the project proceeds. CDC has not yet published a final agreement setting out payment milestones or how the package would be implemented if the campus were developed in stages.

The company says the development could generate construction activity, local procurement opportunities and skilled employment. Those benefits also remain prospective, pending planning approval, financing, customer demand and construction commitments.

Council’s authorisation of the land sale is separate from development consent: the NSW Government remains responsible for determining the State Significant Development application. CDC has planned community information sessions at the Transgrid Discovery Hub in Wagga Wagga as part of its engagement programme, with further engagement expected as the proposal progresses.

stories.content:
Microsoft, Keppel executives say the AI boom is forcing new approaches to power and data centre investment

ARTIFICIAL intelligence may be advancing by the second, but the energy systems needed to power it can take decades to build – a mismatch that is becoming one of the biggest constraints on the global artificial intelligence boom.

Wong Wai Meng, chief executive officer of data centres at Keppel, said there are already insufficient energy systems globally to meet the AI-related demand the company is seeing, even before the industry tackles the question of powering that growth sustainably.

“The energy system takes decades, but AI, innovation and cloud… by the seconds, I would say, is evolving,” he said during a fireside chat with Mark Souza, corporate vice-president and chief technology officer at Microsoft Asia.

They were speaking at Shell’s Powering Progress Together Forum on Friday (Oct 9) at the Marina Bay Sands Expo and Convention Centre, held as part of Shell’s 135th anniversary celebrations.

The discussion was moderated by Aw Kah Peng, chairman of Shell Companies in Singapore, who framed the conversation around the increasingly close relationship between technology and energy.

While Microsoft and Keppel’s data centre business may not immediately come to mind at an energy event, she said, “energy is the first layer of that stack”.

The challenge, the panellists said, is that AI is moving at a pace far quicker than the physical infrastructure supporting it.

For data centres, this goes beyond electricity. Wong said that water, network connectivity, land and financing must also keep pace with growing computing capacity.

He argued that these systems can no longer be planned in isolation.

The infrastructure supporting AI needs to be considered as one interconnected stack, he said, stretching from energy and water through to data centres, chips, applications and, ultimately, the tokens generated by AI models.

At present, however, “every piece basically is in its own… silo”, he said.

## ‘Bring your own power’

That tension is already shaping how governments approach the growth of data centres.

Wong said regulators in different countries are increasingly asking data centre operators and AI companies to “bring your own power”, rather than relying entirely on electricity grids that also serve households and other industries.

He said the principle was understandable, but added that the infrastructure needed to deliver that additional power must also be built.

If gas is part of the solution, for instance, there must be sufficient fuel supply and pipeline capacity, he said.

Policymakers therefore need to think further ahead about how energy infrastructure develops alongside data centre demand, Wong added.

Souza similarly argued that consumers should not have to bear the additional energy costs created by new data centres.

“When we put in a data centre, we are going to take on the extra cost – we are not going to put it to the consumer and the communities that we build in,” he said of Microsoft’s approach.

Companies building data centres also have a responsibility to ensure the communities hosting them benefit, including through jobs, education and investment, Souza added.

Energy remains the more difficult constraint, he said. AI chips require significantly more power, while the supporting cooling infrastructure adds to the overall electricity requirement.

Souza said demand for AI infrastructure is already outstripping supply, with technology companies spending “billions and billions of dollars” to provide customers with the power, space and computing capacity they need.

“That backlog will be there for several years,” he said.

Still, the surge in AI-related power demand could also become part of the solution, Wong said.

He noted that new energy systems require large and reliable customers to underpin investment. Historically, that scale could come from government policy or large commercial users.

AI is now producing a level of demand that could itself support investment in new energy infrastructure, he said.

“Never before have we seen a scale of offtake like demand from AI,” he said, adding that such demand could become the commercial offtaker needed for new energy systems to be developed.

Rather than seeing rapid AI growth and pressure on the energy system as separate problems, Wong argued that they could instead be considered together.

Aw picked up on the point, noting that companies increasingly need to bring different parties together instead of remaining within their traditional industry silos.

## Rethinking the data centre

The speed of AI development is also changing the economics of the data centre business itself, Wong said.

A data centre built seven or eight years ago might have been designed to last 30 years, he noted.

Today, however, some of the technology inside a new facility could need to be replaced within around five years as successive generations of graphics processing units arrive.

While the building itself may remain, Wong said operators need to think differently about how easily individual systems could be changed out.

That has implications not just for engineering, but also for the way investments are depreciated and paid off, he added.

He pointed to cooling systems as an example.

Rather than designing them as largely permanent installations, Wong said data centre operators may need systems that can be swapped out when the requirements of a new generation of chips change.

He likened the approach to replacing individual Lego-like modules, rather than rebuilding an entire system.

The shift also requires regulators and industry to plan further ahead, even as technological requirements continue changing rapidly, he said.

Wong cautioned that short term responses such as requiring operators to provide their own power could become “Band-Aid policies” if they are not accompanied by a longer term infrastructure plan.

“Over the long term, are we creating a very messy infrastructure?” he asked.

A similar challenge arose with Keppel’s floating data centre project, which he said took more than five years to reach the construction stage.

Government agencies including the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore, National Environment Agency and Building and Construction Authority were supportive of the concept, he said.

The difficulty, according to Wong, came from the fact that the project crossed several traditional areas of responsibility.

“Sometimes that silo is a curse when you need to innovate, when you need to cross disciplines,” Wong said.

He suggested that governments could consider how regulatory structures might better accommodate projects that cut across industries and disciplines.

## Keeping up with AI

But infrastructure is only one side of the adjustment, the speakers said. Companies and their workers are also having to change how they operate as AI capabilities improve.

Souza said the companies furthest ahead in AI adoption tend to have strong backing from the top of the organisation.

The same holds true in Asia, he said, although companies in the region face additional challenges including multiple languages, localisation, restrictions on moving data across borders and the availability of computing resources.

He added that while it has become relatively easy to build AI agents, the harder task is deploying them securely and efficiently, while putting the necessary governance around them.

That has to be followed by training and clear use cases, he said, rather than simply giving employees access to AI tools and telling them to experiment.

At Microsoft, even the initial roll-out of its Copilot productivity tools required repeated efforts to encourage adoption, Souza said.

The company shares effective prompts and examples internally, uses elements of gamification and recognises teams that make heavier use of the technology, he added.

Wong said Keppel is similarly trying to push employees to change how they work.

One method is to deliberately create resource constraints and challenge teams to achieve more with the same – or fewer – resources, while asking them to consider how AI could improve productivity, he said.

At the same time, Keppel has invested in AI training and is sharing use cases to give employees ideas about how the technology can be applied in their own functions, he added.

Aw said the harder task may be changing the mindset around learning itself.

Rather than treating training as something employees must find separate time for, organisations need to develop “a state of mind of learning all the time”, she said.

That becomes increasingly important as companies confront concern over whether AI will displace workers.

Souza argued that AI is more likely to replace individual tasks than entire jobs, drawing a parallel with the introduction of calculators.

Companies can use AI primarily to reduce costs and perform the same work with fewer people, he said, or use it to increase what their existing workforce is capable of doing.

“You can be a company that embraces it and does more,” he said. “And I think we all aspire to be that company.”

stories.title: Phaidra partners Aligned on AI data centre operations
stories.summary: The deployment aims to help operators spot faults earlier and manage denser AI workloads with a single view of infrastructure data.
stories.content:
Phaidra has partnered with Aligned Data Centres to deploy its Prism platform across Aligned's data centre portfolio, bringing AI agents into the company's operations teams.

Prism will act as a read-only intelligence layer for data centre operations, drawing on telemetry from building management systems, electrical power monitoring systems and other infrastructure systems, alongside operational documentation. It is designed to identify early-stage irregularities, support root cause analysis and provide guidance through a natural language interface.

Aligned is deploying the system as it manages increasingly dense and dynamic workloads across digital infrastructure. Those workloads create more complex interactions across compute, power, cooling and networking systems, increasing the demands on operations teams.

Phaidra has also integrated NVIDIA DSX Exchange, part of NVIDIA DSX OS, into Prism. According to the companies, the data layer brings together information from mechanical, electrical, power, cooling and IT systems, giving operators a single view of infrastructure data through a conversational interface.

Traditional monitoring tools have generally focused on surfacing raw data rather than providing context for decision-making. The move reflects a wider shift in the data centre sector towards operational software that helps staff interpret large volumes of facility data as sites grow more complex.

For Aligned, the deployment extends investment in tools for day-to-day operations, commissioning and quality assurance. Michael Welch, Chief Technology Officer of Aligned Data Centres, linked the technology to the practical demands operators face as facilities evolve.

"Data center environments are more dynamic and advanced than ever before. To meet this moment, we owe it to our operators to put the best tools in their hands," said Michael Welch, Chief Technology Officer, Aligned Data Centres.

"Assistive intelligence systems like Phaidra Prism don't replace our teams' expertise - they amplify it, surfacing critical context in real time so our operators can act with greater speed and precision. Beyond daily operations, this technology adds tremendous value by streamlining new capacity commissioning and elevating quality assurance across our portfolio. Ultimately, this partnership is an investment in our people as much as our infrastructure," Welch said.

### Operational focus

The agreement shows how AI is being applied in data centres beyond design and construction. Operators are under pressure to maintain reliable performance while managing more demanding workloads, and suppliers are increasingly positioning AI tools as a way to help teams respond more quickly to irregularities in complex facilities.

Phaidra said its approach centres on facility-specific intelligence for operations teams. The company describes its software as a way to unify information often split across separate systems, a longstanding issue in data centre environments where mechanical, electrical and IT data can sit in different operational silos.

Jim Gao, Chief Executive Officer and Co-founder of Phaidra, said the partnership is intended to align operational practices with the increasing complexity of digital infrastructure.

"As digital infrastructure becomes increasingly sophisticated and dynamic, our operational approach must also evolve. Aligned has built industry-leading infrastructure that can adapt to the demands of high-density computing, and together we're bringing that same adaptability to data center operations - helping teams run facilities with greater speed, efficiency, and reliability," said Jim Gao, Chief Executive Officer and Co-founder, Phaidra.

The deployment also highlights the growing role of platform providers such as NVIDIA in the data centre software stack. By using DSX Exchange as a common data layer, Prism is intended to consolidate inputs from multiple infrastructure domains into a single operational view for staff managing facilities in real time.

As operators expand capacity for AI and other intensive workloads, the operational side of the business is becoming a bigger focus for technology vendors. The system is intended to help teams prioritise operational needs and access the information required for faster decisions.

Prior to her lengthy stint at Google, she worked in supply chain roles at Infinera, PowerFile, and supercomputing firm SGI.

stories.title: Microchip Technology updates its networking and storage products to better support AI and HPC workloads
stories.summary: Expanded data center portfolio will help customers address multiple infrastructure challenges, the company said
stories.content:
Microchip Technology has expanded its data center solutions portfolio by enhancing its networking and storage offerings to support artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC) applications.

The additions include the Switchtec PCIe 6.0 Low-Lane-Count (LLC) switch, an updated Flashtec PCIe Gen 5 NVMe 5016 SSD controller, and an enhanced Adaptec SmartRAID 4300 family of NVMe RAID storage accelerators.

Microchip said the LLC switch has been designed for space- and power-constrained systems, providing up to 64 PCIe Gen 6 lanes and 32 ports, with flexible two-, four-, eight-, and 16-bifurcation options. The switch also incorporates direct memory access technology to support peer-to-peer data transfers between connected devices while reducing host CPU involvement, the company said, adding that it has also extended the same PCIe multicast and partitioning functions to the switch as can already be found in Microchip’s larger PCIe Gen 6 switch product portfolio.

Meanwhile, the updates to Microchip’s storage products will see its Flashtec PCIe Gen 5 NVMe 5016 SSD controller offer advanced virtualization, quality of service management, and programmability, to help optimize performance across enterprise, hyperscale, and AI deployments.

The company’s family of Adaptec SmartRAID 4300 NVMe RAID storage accelerators has also been upgraded, offering improved storage security and data protection, while minimizing downtime. Microchip has further added self-encrypting drives with both local and remote key management in RAID 6 and RAID 60 configurations for increased resiliency and security.

“Customers are looking for technology partners that can address multiple challenges across the infrastructure stack while helping simplify design and accelerate deployment,” said Brian McCarson, corporate VP and GM of Microchip’s data center solutions unit. “By continuing to expand our portfolio, we're providing the building blocks needed to create more efficient, secure, and adaptable platforms for today’s increasingly distributed and data-intensive computing environments.”

stories.title: FERC approves PJM's request to create data center database
stories.summary: Rejects separate request to curtail power to data centers during periods of grid stress
stories.content:
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) has approved PJM Interconnection's request to develop a data center database across its footprint.

The new database is expected to improve how PJM plans for data centers. It will give the Regional Transmission Operator (RTO) more detail on each site, including location, power providers, in-service dates, and load ramp-up timelines, as well as backup generation and fuel supply.

Although FERC approved the creation of a database, it rejected several other provisions PJM requested to manage data center load, including allowing it to temporarily shut off grid power to the facilities to avoid blackouts during peak demand.

In a filing, the regulatory body said PJM could submit a revised curtailment plan, but it would have to address several issues to gain approval, including why data centers would be shut off instead of other large industrial users. FERC said it rejected the plan because it strayed outside the RTO’s authority.

PJM, which is the largest RTO in the US, has been grappling with huge data center demand across its footprint, which includes data center hotspots such as Virginia and Ohio. This has led to price increases and impacted grid reliability, including a large-scale voltage disturbance in July, which saw more than 3GW of power being brought offline.

PJM only expects data center demand across its footprint to rise in the coming years, with the RTO projecting electricity requirements from the sector to triple by 2030 to 29GW across its Midwest and Mid-Atlantic territory.

To account for the huge demand, the RTO has set out a range of proposals. For example, in August, the grid operator proposed that all new data center customers with a capacity of 50MW or more must pay for the new power generation needed to support their facilities. Several states and utilities have already imposed similar rules to prevent cost shifting onto regular ratepayers.

stories.title: Legrand to integrate Karman AI platform into data center PDUs and power shelves
stories.summary: First deal following Karman's rebrand
stories.content:
Energy infrastructure AI platform Karman (formerly known as Utilidata) has partnered with French industrial group Legrand to integrate Karman into its data center power distribution product lines.

According to the companies, this will include Legrand's intelligent AC rack PDUs and DC power shelves, which it claims are designed for high-density AI data centers.

Karman’s platform utilizes AI to provide real-time visibility for grid operators and data center firms. It works by identifying and managing distributed energy resources, which it claims enhances resiliency and offsets the need for future infrastructure investments. The platform can integrate with smart meters, providing AI solutions for utility companies and their customers.

The company developed the platform using a custom version of the Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano, which it claims provides 100 times the processing power of other meter-based solutions. The platform can connect to millions of endpoints and coordinate them to monitor and react to real-time conditions.

According to the partners, the deployment could allow Legrand’s data center customers to power more compute and generate 50 percent or more AI tokens using the same provisioned power.

"By partnering with Karman, Legrand continues to demonstrate its technological leadership and innovation by delivering additional value to data center operators,” said Swen Anderson, CTO of Legrand Data Power and Control Division.

“We’re providing data centers with the tools to unlock stranded power and deliver measurable competitive advantages and increased revenue.”

“Power continues to be the primary limiting factor to data center capacity expansion. Yet, a large portion of provisioned power in data centers goes untapped,” added Josh Brumberger, CEO of Karman. “This partnership with Legrand changes that. By embedding Karman into Legrand’s power distribution products, data center operators can now utilize that power to expand capacity immediately, while reducing the price per GPU hour.”

Karman was rebranded earlier this month, formerly operating under the name Utilidata.

In June, the firm raised $60.3 million in Series C funding to scale its platform, led by Renown Capital Partners, with participation from Quanta, Nvidia, and existing investor Keyframe Capital.

stories.title: VivoPower starts construction at 42MW Mo i Rana data center in Norway
stories.summary: To spin off 2.2GW non-Nordic AI data center portfolio into a new listed firm
stories.content:
VivoPower, a powered land and data center developer, has commenced the first phase of construction at its 42MW Mo i Rana data center in northern Norway.

The company said the works will include demolishing existing structures, enabling works, and constructing the main building superstructure, among other elements. Local Mo i Rana contractors will deliver the works and complete them ahead of the facility's mechanical and electrical fit-out, for which VivoPower has conducted a tender review process.

The company also revealed that it has selected what it described as “a global AI industry leader” as its preferred AI tenant for the facility. It did not disclose the tenant's identity.

The facility is a former cryptocurrency mining site that Vivo acquired from Cowa in April. Bitfury originally constructed the facility in 2018. According to Vivo, the data center conversion is being completed with the aim of capturing waste heat from its cooling systems for reuse. The company said that it is working directly with a local district heating provider and European specialist firms to evaluate how the heat can be used, including supplying district heating services and heat-intensive industries.

"We have deliberately engaged with the local construction supply chain, and we are delighted to be working with Mo i Rana firms such as Øijord & Aanes, IMTAS and TH Blikk. Their skills and local knowledge will be invaluable as we move from site works towards the mechanical and electrical fit-out phase. We remain committed to delivering on a ready-for-service (RFS) date as expeditiously as possible but without compromising quality and safety given the long-duration nature of the infrastructure asset being built," said Shane Whelan, chief real estate officer, VivoPower.

The company did not specify a completion date for the construction works. *DCD* has reached out for further information.

## New non-Nordic platform

Alongside the start of construction, VivoPower also announced the formation of a new, separate AI infrastructure firm that will manage its non-Nordic AI data center portfolio and pipeline.

The new company will be headquartered in Singapore and funded through a targeted pre-IPO institutional and sovereign investment round followed by a planned primary listing on the London Stock Exchange and a secondary listing on the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange.

According to the company, it will house the firm's non-Nordic AI data center infrastructure portfolio, which Vivo claims comprises more than 2.2GW of assets and development opportunities located primarily across the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, and the Philippines. The company said that the portfolio includes ready-to-build assets, secured powered-land positions, MoU-stage sites, and prospective sites.

"The Board has approved the establishment of a separately listed Platform to hold and independently capitalize the non-Nordic AI data center portfolio which our team has assembled through long-standing sovereign and government relationships across the GCC and ASEAN regions,” said Kevin Chin, executive chairman and CEO of VivoPower.

“At present, this comprises in excess of 2.2GW of assets and development opportunities located primarily across the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, and the Philippines. We believe this strategy and structure best matches these assets with the right sovereign and institutional capital, which may unlock incremental value for VivoPower shareholders. This is by virtue of VivoPower retaining de facto control of the Platform and preserving shareholder exposure to the non-Nordic upside, without VivoPower having to fund the associated construction capital expenditure."

VivoPower, founded in 2014 and listed on the Nasdaq since 2016, operates across the UK, Australia, North America, Europe, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. The company’s operations span electric mobility, renewable power applications, and digital asset infrastructure, with a growing focus on AI computing.

stories.summary: Big Watt Digital, an integrated power and digital infrastructure company, together with its co-development partner PowerHouse Data Centers, a real estate and digital infrastructure developer and a division of American Real Estate Partners (AREP), has announced that it has secured approval of its development agreement for the Taylor Technology Campus project just outside the city […]
stories.content:
Big Watt Digital, an integrated power and digital infrastructure company, together with its co-development partner PowerHouse Data Centers, a real estate and digital infrastructure developer and a division of American Real Estate Partners (AREP), has announced that it has secured approval of its development agreement for the Taylor Technology Campus project just outside the city of Taylor, Texas.

The project, a joint venture between Big Watt Digital and PowerHouse Data Centers according to a press release, will be set on a 664-acre site in Taylor, Texas. The campus will have the potential to support up to one gigawatt of hyperscale data center capacity.

“The introduction of the Taylor site demonstrates Big Watt and PowerHouse’s immediate progress along with what the company was built to do: bring power and digital infrastructure together from the outset to deliver speed, scale and certainty for the AI economy,” said Alex Hern, Big Watt Digital Co-founder and Co-Chief Executive Officer.

The development agreement that has been approved provides for project-specific standards governing water use, stormwater management, site design, landscaping, setbacks, as well as lighting and noise. The plan also includes developer-funded improvements to the City of Taylor’s reclaimed-water infrastructure among other enhanced standards in several areas.

On power, the Taylor Technology Campus plans to utilize dedicated, behind-the-meter power generation, leaning on natural gas resources capable of supporting large-scale operations. Power availability at the campus is targeted for the first half of 2028, aligning power delivery with data center deployment schedules.

“By pairing digital infrastructure with dedicated, behind-the-meter power, we are designing for and addressing one of the biggest constraints facing data center development today — access to reliable power — without relying solely on incremental grid capacity,” added Hern.

“Austin is one of the most dynamic technology markets in the country, and the Taylor Technology Campus project gives us a strategically positioned platform to support the next generation of AI and hyperscale computing while delivering meaningful economic benefits to Taylor and the broader region,” said Keith Meyer, Big Watt Digital President.

According to Meyer, the project will bring private investment, employment opportunities, and economic activity to the local community. On that, the co-developers state that the campus is being planned with consideration for the surrounding community and local resources.

Power availability is a massive constraint in Texas. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) is tracking 438,000 MW of large load requests, nearly 89 percent of which are for data centers. As w.media reported in September, ERCOT granted base load approval to several data center developers including IREN, Hut 8, CleanSpark, and Galaxy Digital as part of its Batch Zero process. By opting for a behind-the-meter power generation solution, the Taylor Technology Campus may avoid the long delays associated with grid connection in the Lone Star State.

stories.title: NinjaTech launches fixed-price AI platform for enterprises
stories.summary: Enterprises can now run AI agents in their own cloud or data centre without unpredictable usage charges, easing cost and data-control concerns.
stories.content:
Tue, 13th Oct 2026 (Yesterday)
NinjaTech AI has launched SuperNinja Enterprise, an AI workforce platform that companies can run in their own cloud environments. It is sold at a fixed annual price that includes computing capacity.

The Palo Alto-based company says the platform lets businesses deploy AI agents inside their own cloud or data centre rather than relying on an external service. It uses open-weight models and also supports models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

SuperNinja Enterprise combines software, model-serving infrastructure and GPU-backed inference capacity under one contract. Customers can deploy the system on single-tenant capacity through Microsoft with Fireworks AI or AWS, while organisations with stricter security requirements can choose a licensed deployment in an air-gapped environment using their own hardware.

The launch comes as companies look to move beyond small AI trials while keeping tighter control over spending and data handling. Usage-based pricing has made it difficult for many businesses to forecast costs as AI agents take on longer-running tasks and consume more computing resources than simple chatbot interactions.

### Cost model

NinjaTech says organisations running open-weight models on reserved capacity can reduce end-to-end costs to about one-tenth of comparable deployments based on frontier lab models. The company is positioning the offer as an alternative to per-token billing, with annual pricing designed to stay stable as usage rises.

That pricing model addresses a central concern for large companies testing AI tools at scale. Businesses often have to secure GPU capacity, deploy model-serving systems and source applications through separate suppliers, adding cost uncertainty and procurement complexity.

Packages are sized for 100, 500 or 1,000 AI employees. The platform also integrates with Slack and Microsoft Teams, allowing workers to use the system through tools already common in the workplace.

### Data control

NinjaTech is also emphasising data residency and separation. Enterprise data stays within the customer's own environment and is not pooled to train external models, a point likely to matter in sectors handling regulated or commercially sensitive information.

"With SuperNinja Enterprise, your CISO can rest assured data never goes outside your own walls," said Babak Pahlavan, Chief Executive Officer of NinjaTech AI. "Your CFO gets an AI bill that doesn't move. And everyone sleeps well, knowing you can scale AI without waking up to skyrocketing costs."

For the first time, NinjaTech is supplying the GPU and inference capacity for the platform rather than leaving customers to assemble those components themselves. In practice, that means buyers get the AI software and the underlying computing arrangement under one commercial agreement.

### Partners involved

Healthcare customers will work with Optimum HealthcareIT for integration, while other enterprise customers will work with Infosys. Infosys is also described by NinjaTech as an investor and implementation partner.

The product keeps model choice open, allowing customers to move workflows between open-weight systems and proprietary models. That approach reflects a broader enterprise effort to avoid dependence on a single model provider as pricing, performance and policy terms continue to shift across the AI market.

NinjaTech says many enterprise AI projects remain stuck at the pilot stage because finance teams struggle to predict usage-based charges and security teams resist sending sensitive workloads to outside providers. It argues that placing the system inside a customer-controlled environment with fixed annual pricing removes both barriers.

"Most vendors keep AI on a usage meter," said Pahlavan. "We give enterprises predictable capacity and costs, so adoption can spread across the organisation instead of stopping at a pilot."
